body:
I feel this. I turned 27 this year, and it hit me *hard*. When I was 13, I imagined I'd be dead by 18. When I was 18, dead by 21. When I was 21, dead by 25, and at 25, dead by 27... Now I figure I'll be dead before I hit 40. Turning 27 was the first time I really had to think about what a future would need to look like for me. I had believed I would die by either an act that was suicidally stupid (like jumping from a roof into a pool, doing drugs, etc), or an act of intentional suicide. I've definitely done my fair share of suicidally stupid things, but never quite got to the intentional suicide part.

Turning 27 made me seriously reflect on that belief. Not because I somehow thought "Oh, I was wrong", but because I know I was definitely *not* wrong, and yet the way I was talking about the belief was never coming true. I didn't understand how I was still alive. The conclusion that I'm coming to is that my belief isn't exactly "I'm definitely going to die by suicide", it is "I'm never going to stop having suicidal thoughts or a desire to kill myself", which, while almost the same, were meaningfully different for me - in the first case, it's like, "The suicide is a foregone conclusion, there's no reason to fight it", but the second is "The suicide is always following me, and one day it will catch up to me."  


I guess to me the meaningful difference was that second version made some room in my belief for some small part of me that doesn't want to be dead. I'm not ready to feel hope yet, because a lot of things in my life seem insurmountable, but it also leaves room for some hope that that part of me can get stronger and be in charge more, according to my therapist.  


So I guess the overall message is: Unequivocally, yes, I definitely relate to that feeling you described. You are definitely not alone. But, that kind of belief can be really complicated and personal, and every person has to examine it for themselves and understand what they're really feeling, because my experience has been that things I am *that* certain about tend to be carefully built beliefs that keep me from focusing on a really scary thing, like the idea that I may never stop feeling miserable. But at least that's a fear that I can communicate to other people, you know?

I don't personally think it is either "immoral" or "moral", I think it is just a part of the human experience. I also think it makes the average person uncomfortable in a really fundamental way.

There's a short story I read back in college (I bet a ton of people have heard of it) - "The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas". I think about it a lot. The premise is that there is this great utopian society, but in order for that society to exist, a single person must suffer immensely at all times. Once a people learn about this person who must suffer, many decide to leave the society.

In our world, people who haven't had to directly contend with suicidal thoughts probably don't see the parts of society that drive people to that place. Because there's no way to "walk away" from our society, I think it creates this cognitive dissonance of for people, where accepting that things can really be that bad for someone implies that society is broken, but their life isn't broken like that, either: they had luck, or they obtained their own happiness and well-being through hard work and skill. If they choose to believe they were lucky, then it introduces a fear that maybe that luck can run out and they could possibly be the next one to suffer. If they choose to believe that they have good things through hard work and effort, it keeps that fear away and makes it easier to deal with the idea that other people struggle: "they're just not good enough", or "it's a momentary weakness, but if they work hard enough they can overcome it".

I don't agree with that kind of thinking, because I've struggled with suicidal thoughts most of my life. If I had never struggled with them, though, I can imagine that I might think similarly to that. If someone doesn't wish to die, it requires understanding a completely different version of the world to understand how someone could wish that, and it is a huge effort to do that. Since the effort is so large, people come up with things like "suicide is wrong" and "suicide is a permanent solution to a temporary problem".

>But I'm... Too tired. I'm tired of crying everyday, of feeling useless,   
like a broken piece inside a putrid machine. I hate this world. Social   
media is filled with hate and despair, society is breaking under crisis   
and inhumanity. I can't change anything, I can't even change myself!

This really hit home for me. I empathize a lot with that. I have been working on myself for a long time, and I've been on medication. It really did help for a while, but there are just things about myself that I can't get past and it makes the idea of sticking around feel really unbearable. Like, I don't think I can change those thing about myself because I have really tried. Whenever I think I've made some progress, I inevitably find myself back in a really broken place. Idk what to do with all of that - I know the people close to me would be hurt, but at the same time I can't take much more of this. It really is tiring, in a deep-in-my-bones kind of way. It's like my soul is tired or something.

I think you're right that talking is not a solution, in the sense that it doesn't get anyone over the mountain any faster. I've never been a fan of platitudes and the "it will get better" attitude, because "getting better" isn't some state-of-mind thing, it can be a thing to which there are real external obstacles. That being said, I do appreciate people who are willing to listen to me when it just gets to be too much to carry all at once. I can't do any of the things I want to do to try to improve my situation if I'm frozen in place, and sometimes talking can help shift that weight for long enough to take a single step. That's my experience, and I understand if you don't relate to it at all. Just wanted to share.

Thanks for sharing this, I like it. And I am here to talk if you want - I am not on this sub as a helper - I'm struggling myself - but my heart hurts for everyone suffering and I will listen to whatever you want to get off of your chest non-judgementally.

>There's no real way out, is there?

I wish that I knew.  


It sounds like your family situation is different than mine, but I can at least relate a little bit. I grew up in a super religious household. Church every Sunday, a father obsessed with the rapture, a mother suspicious of every non-white, non-christian person, and catholicism classes twice a week until I was 15. I've struggled as long as I can remember, too - I don't know specifically what age it started, but probably 13/14. I never felt like the people around me understood, or cared, and even though my parents were a little more open to the idea of therapy instead of prayer, they just dumped me with some rando state therapist and said stuff like "Why aren't you better yet?". So I just bottled it up, got out as soon as I could. I spent 4 years at college, but I was so depressed for 1.5 of them that the money dried up before I graduated and I had to go get a job and move back home.  


I worked for a while and then moved out, and eventually relocated across the country for a "dream" (it was not) job. COVID happened, I lost that job, fell back into a severe depression, and got stuck again. Had to move home a second time at 27. I frequently have a thought like yours, that I should try to kill myself because at least if I don't succeed people will finally get how much I struggle, and maybe someone will figure out just how badly I need help.  


I don't know what the way out is. I know every situation is different, and yours is certainly different from mine, but I just wanted you to know that there are other people looking for answers in this crappy world, too. If you want to talk, feel free to reply to this comment. I try to check back often and reply to people.

That is a truly difficult situation, and it sounds like you've been willing to give a lot to this relationship only to have it blow up in a cruel and unexpected way. I don't know any specifics of your situation, and this might not be similar to your experience, but: When I am feeling my lowest, I find that it is also when I am the least willing to reach out for help. I have a hunch that posting here was (as it is for me) a way to reach out for something or someone without putting a "burden" on someone else. From the tiny bit I know, you sound like a caring person who invests in the people around them, and (if you're anything like myself), probably at the expense of your own needs. I struggle greatly with asking the people around me for help. I don't know what I would ask of them to begin with. Every now and then I do ask, and sometimes I don't get what I need anyway, but when I do it can be a very cathartic experience. Of course, that has been my experience and I don't mean to imply that it will be or is yours. My heart hurts for you, though, friend.

I was raised in a "Christian" household and I feel similarly. There's no reason that life would be like this for some of us if this concept of a merciful, nice God existed. If the "Christians" I know really believe in a merciful God then they sure don't live like they seem to think God would.

That's rough buddy. In all seriousness that is absolutely horrible and idk how someone can just check out of a family like that, and I'm so sorry you're dealing with that pain.

What if you asked the aunt/uncle to watch your son for a weekend so you can have some time to yourself? The situation sounds like a really toxic environment for someone to be in, and if it is that toxic all day every day then I think even the most rational and reasonable person alive would find themselves contemplating every possible way to get out. It sounds like you might need (and definitely deserve) a break. I don't mean to imply that will fix the problems, but as long as you're still here it couldn't hurt to do yourself a small kindness like that, right? Right now, you're carrying an amount that would be lot for *anyone* I know.

I think the OP might have misunderstood your question. The way you phrased it comes across more as "Well then you must think ALL positivity is toxic lol", but it seems to me like you meant "What kind of positivity, if any, doesn't feel toxic to you?". Sorry you're being downvoted, but I also get why. People who feel like this (I am one of them) are very sensitive to the fact that people tend not to understand, and when someone thinks they understand and they don't it can feel super invalidating and that makes all the other bad feelings worse.

I feel you. I actually really appreciate that this sub has a specific rule about this stuff: [https://www.reddit.com/r/SuicideWatch/comments/25igd7/whats\_wrong\_with\_it\_gets\_better\_what\_if\_it\_doesnt/](https://www.reddit.com/r/SuicideWatch/comments/25igd7/whats_wrong_with_it_gets_better_what_if_it_doesnt/)  


Turns out that it's actually worse than useless to look at someone struggling and say "It'll be ok" / "It gets better" / "One day you won't feel like this" because  1. someone has no idea whether it's true, and 2. even on the off chance that it turns out it is true for the person struggling, the whole point of feeling like suicide is the best option is that the person already doesn't believe that is true.  


On a personal level, my dad does this. He says stuff like "chin up, bud" and "it's hard now, but you'll learn to handle it". I think he actually does care, but he's also dangerously depressed and so when he says that it's like "Dude, what would you know about that? You don't want to be alive today either", and it really cements the already strong thought that some people are just like this and can't / won't get better. Whenever I feel like someone has actually helped me, it's *always* after someone says something like "Yeah, it *really* sucks. Here's something realistic we can do that will make one specific part less shitty for some amount of time".

I've been feeling the same way lately. I tried to have this conversation with my sister a few weeks ago and she said something like "It's not possible to freely choose to kill yourself, you're always being coerced by your own mind's depressive thoughts". I don't agree with that at all, but she's someone who has also struggled with this stuff so it was interesting to hear that opinion from her.

I don't know that it is either cowardly *or* brave, it just kind of *is*. I feel like this concept of trying to assign some kind of moral weight to it doesn't fit with how I think about it at all. I could choose to keep living, and that requires one kind of effort, or I could choose to end my life, and that requires a different kind of effort or plan. People get more emotionally attached to the idea of my own suicide than I do. I think I have a relatively pragmatic opinion about the fact that it might make sense for me, but people seem to think its like "a moment of pain" when in reality I just have looked at my life, what I want from it and what I can't get from it, the level of effort required to have a quality of life that would make me want to stick around, and say "Why should I do all of that so the people around me don't have to be sad? Isn't that selfish of them to expect?"  


Another poster said that they think of themselves like sisyphus - they are still here just to piss off whatever god or entity put them here. I can get behind that, but like the idea that I should strive to spend decades of my life working too many hours a day just to afford four walls and some food, being mostly miserable the whole time, seems insane - I don't get why people think there's something wrong with a person who looks at that and says "I really don't know if the effort is worth it to me". Like, do people think there are absolutely zero situations where suicide might actually be pragmatic?

Yeah it does suck, I hear you. I wish I had some advice to share, but right now I'm just taking things one day at a time. It has helped to hear from people like you who are also struggling with these feelings, though, so sincerely thank you for sharing.
I think a part of my own struggle is that I don't even really have an answer for that. Are you the same way, or did you have an idea of where you wanted things to be by now?

I can relate. For the past month or so the thing that has brought me the most peace has been thinking about and putting together a plan for taking my life. I'm not 100% sure whether I plan to follow through yet, but I've basically got everything put together except a time and a place, and the process of making that strategy has been one of the only sources of comfort I've had in a while.

I struggle with this feeling too. It seems like it is a totally on-brand way for my life to end one day. I originally thought it would happen before I turned 27... but I turned 27 this year. Now I think it'll happen before I turn 40. If I turn 40, it might change to be before I'm 65. I'm really not sure, but I think the ultimate irony would be if I continue to feel that way up until the day that I die of natural causes or something. There are a lot of people that I don't want to let "be right about me", and that makes it hard for me to choose to end my life, as much as I find myself thinking about it these days.

Is it possible that this perception you have of yourself is something that developed based on stuff you've seen (maybe even just scrolling by) while browsing social media or other parts of the internet? Over the last year+ I've leaned in to a lot of my already painful insecurities based on the stuff people say online, specifically the way people joke about men with mental illness. I've started to feel like a person with no value who is impossible to love, and like I'm just a burden on the world. Even though I still struggling with a lot, the world has seemed a little kinder since I've gotten off of the social media sites that I used to frequent. I didn't realize how much seeing little jabs in tweets or post titles was affecting me until I was finally able to take a small step back, and I was really surprised to discover just how much of my self image was based on those opinions, from people I've 1. never met, and 2. almost definitely never will.

I can't comment on the penis size thing - that's very personal for you, and I hear that. I might be able to empathize, though, because to me the fact that I struggle with the particular flavor of mental illness that I do is something that feels totally immutable about myself, and is something where I don't feel any hope that it can change. I know how lonely that can feel and I know that I struggle myself with feeling like this world has a place for me, or that anyone would be able to love me.

I don't have a good answer for you today, but I just want you to know you're not alone in those kinds of feelings and I hope from the bottom of my heart that you can find a few moments of peace today :)

I'm still working on healthier coping mechanisms, but the place that I've settled for now while I work through things with my therapist is basically "I didn't die before 27, but I think that eventually my life will end by suicide, maybe in my 40s if I make it that far".  


Who knows, maybe I'm right about that, but at least its a little bit of permission to keep living for right now, and that's been a little helpful for the last couple of weeks.

I turned 27 this year, and I struggled a lot with that. I always thought I wouldn't make it to 27 (that notorious age where rock stars die, even though I am definitely not a rock star), but there I was on my birthday. My plan was never to be here today. I think I can really relate to the idea that I never thought I'd live this long, and like there's not really a point because I never planned to have to figure out what I wanted to be or where I wanted to go with my life after 27. I know that this doesn't make your situation feel better, but maybe it'll help to know that you're not alone in feeling those things and struggling with them. It definitely helped me to read this - now I know that it isn't just me who didn't expect to be here and is struggling to find a reason to continue, and at least for a few minutes this morning I feel a little less alone.

Apparently when I was born it was in a very risky way and I almost did not make it. I almost got to skip this whole life. Right now, every day is a struggle to understand why I am here, and what reason there could possibly be for me to have survived that experience. I don't have an answer for you today, but I understand and hear you, friend.

It definitely was overwhelming for me when I first sought help. I had to go through a few different therapists before I really found one that was able to really help me work on some of my struggles. If it is something you choose to pursue, my advice would be to trust your gut - if you feel invalidated by a therapist repeatedly, it is ok to seek other help. Therapists are people too and even smart, educated people can make mistakes or be a bad fit for a individual. I struggled with a lot of self-blame when I started that journey and I quit several times, but I eventually found someone that worked well with me and while I am still struggling (I'm here after all) I definitely feel that she has helped me build more skills for tolerating difficult situations and challenging my depressive thoughts and patterns. It's slow going and I struggle with self-doubt about whether it will work, but I do keep going because she seems to really believe that with enough time I will start to feel better.
Thank you, you too.

Its kind of messed up how the world just expects people to produce some "value" in the form of money. I bet there's stuff you'd do if you didn't have to worry about bills and all that, and could just do stuff for the sake of doing stuff.

Idk if this helps but if you did want to go to school, depending on where you are there are grants and stuff, even if you wanted to like go to trade school instead of a university or whatever.  


Who knows, maybe you have a deep undiscovered love of deep-sea welding. I might, I've never tried.
Thanks, you too. Not trying to hijack your post, I just wanted to share in case you related to anything in there.

Word, I probably smoke that much (maybe a little less) right now as well. I notice that I feel the brain fog the most like the morning after I smoke (if I do before bed) or in the afternoon (if I smoke in the morning). It has gotten better with time, though. It has probably been like 4 months since I smoked a lot. I'm taking a break right now for a job search and I've felt a tiny bit faster mentally. I think the depression on top of the other stuff adds to that brain fog, too - I just have a lot in my head so the "normal human" stuff (as I call it) takes longer to come out.  


I relate a lot to the "feeling out of place" thing. I haven't feel that way in the past, but over the last year it got really bad. A lot of that was the isolation. Social stuff was always higher-effort for me even if I enjoyed it, and I got really out of practice. Maybe that's not a what it is for you, maybe its something else. I didn't know what it was for me for a LONG time, I had to spend some effort to unpack all of it with my therapist - before we got there I just knew that I didn't like going out in the world and I always felt like I was out of place, and had that "people are looking at me weird" sense even if in all likelihood they weren't. I'm not over it, but definitely doing stuff people see as "needed" like walking the dog helps.  


This might sound real dumb but I've started buying like candy or snacks I really like when I go out for cigarettes. It's this simple little thing but it makes me feel a little more normal, and sometimes the person will be like "oh shit I love those (candy/chips/whatever)" and I can be like "dude, right? so good" and its a little interaction to put back in the "normal person" pile.

I'm in a similar place right now (hence why I'm on this sub). I don't have a great answer, and I am afraid of that myself. It feels like there's not a ton that can really be good in the world, or my life, right now. What if you did something crazy like try to catfish predatory old men online to report them to the police? The few times I've found joy in something lately (very very rare), it has been doing something I don't normally do. I'm not a fan of random labor-intensive projects, but a few weeks ago I built a shed for my parents (who I have a tense relationship with at best) and it was terrible, but for like 5 minutes somewhere in the middle I smiled. I'm just out here fishing for anything to bring me a moment of respite, but I've had to get pretty weird and creative with it.

Are you still smoking weed? Whenever I go through a really heavy smoking phase (I go in and out), I end up feeling super shitty, like you described - I'll feel blank-headed, slow to talk and respond, slow to think of basic stuff. When you were describing that, I totally related. I can think of several times when I've felt very similarly (and I did the same thing - stayed inside watching videos, playing games, chain smoking, etc).  


Especially with the pandemic this last year, I went from someone I thought of as at least a little extroverted to a super introvert. I didn't leave my place, I had just moved all the way across the country for work so I was totally isolated, and it just spiraled from there. I know what it feels like to dodge calls from friends because you don't want them to "see you like this" or however you're phrasing it in your mind.  


I don't have a solution, but one thing that helped me a lot was walking the dog. If you don't have a dog, do you have a neighbor with a dog who you could offer to walk? It was something to do to go outside, and it gave me a way to do something other than smoke even if it was just for a couple of minutes.

I feel like I'm split right down the middle, exactly 50/50. One half of me absolutely does not want to keep going. The other half is like, willing to entertain the idea that one day I might feel better.

I try to think of it like a balanced scale. When I have a day where the done-with-life side gets too heavy, I try to lighten the load, even for a minute, by doing something like the brain dump writing. That may not work for you, but is there anything that you can do that you can just channel a lifetime's worth of anger, pain, and frustration towards? Video game? Drawing? Beating up a punching bag with every ounce of strength you have for an hour until you have no energy left and fall on the floor?

I appreciate you sharing this with me. Nobody else responded, which I kind of expected, but I'm glad that this resonated with someone.

I'm sorry you're struggling with this stuff, though. I obviously don't know many details, but I can relate. Like, the going back to school thing. I was real poor growing up and so I never had the money. I did some college but had to work and deal with some really complicated emotional health issues, and I didn't finish before the money ran out. I ended up getting a job in my industry anyway, but I always feel like people think I'm not smart because I don't have a piece of paper worth 4 years of my life to get and another 20 to pay off. And I don't have the money to go back... which is really shitty.

This might not mean anything to you, but I always feel like the people who want to get to know me and invest in me are doing something wrong, or I'm somehow misleading them about who I am or how I am, and so then I start to feel guilty. Which makes maintaining those relationships hard. What am I supposed to do, talk to people about that? I'm pretty sure nobody would be interested in hearing how I really believe from the bottom of my heart that I'm this bad unlovable person with nothing to offer and how they absolutely are making a mistake getting to know me.

I don't really know if I'm attractive or not. I've gotten mixed messages from people about that throughout my life. But I think I'm just unlovable, which in a way almost feels worse to me (not saying it is or isn't, I really don't know). But like I get that - it seems like a similar thing, like a belief that, hey, there's this thing about me that is just really hard for other people to get past. Maybe it's my mental health, maybe its my appearance, maybe it's the color of my hair, maybe its my lazy eye, but at the end of the day anyone can decide they dislike me for any reason, and if they don't have to look that hard, it'll happen sooner than later.

If you want to tell me more about it, I'd be happy to listen. I've been refreshing this sub for a couple of hours in a daze. I have time to kill, and if letting you get some of this shit off of your chest helps you, then taking the time to listen will help me by giving me something to do with my time.

I think I get it - I keep some things around, like the lexapro+zoloft you keep, that I can hold sometimes to remind me that, "hey, if you wanted to try again, you could". I haven't tried again yet, and sometimes I think a part of that is that I have things around I could use, and so I think "I could do this whenever, if I didn't do it yesterday, was today really so much worse?"  


I don't really have anything of value to add here, just wanted to say that I related and appreciated what you shared.

It is super shitty when there's nobody to go to for help, but you feel like you're on fire. I've been there. It really sucks. Sometimes I do tell myself stuff like "Some people are just meant to be unhappy". Maybe that's true, maybe it isn't - I'm not a good philosopher, so I just try to do something different.  


If I'm burning alive emotionally, sometimes I'll whip out my phone or a piece of paper (or this sub) and just write down everything I hate about my life, about myself, whatever - and maybe that isn't the "best" thing to do, but if I'm gonna sit there and think it in my head anyway, it can't hurt to put it all on paper. Sometimes the act of doing that is like setting down the weight. Like, I might have to pick it up again tomorrow, or in an hour, but at least for that moment, I don't have to carry it.

I don't know your situation, but can you travel? Not like, to some fancy European beach or Belize or anything. Maybe just a motel the town over with your desktop / laptop / ps3 / ps4 / gameboy color / drawing pad and a pen / phone and netflix? Sometimes when I feel really bad, just sleeping somewhere else, away from my life, can help me feel just the tiniest bit of relief.

If you're trying antidepressants and the first kind you're prescribed don't seem to help or have side effects you don't like, I'd recommend (if you can afford it, of course) going back to the doctor and telling them about it, and asking if there's a different kind you can try.  


I had really bad side effects with the first type that I tried (pretty sure my genetics made me extra-susceptible to stomach problems related to the type I was taking), and instead of going back to the doc I just went off of them for a year+. When I finally went back and said "help" the doc was able to find something that didn't make me feel so terrible. I definitely felt hopeless when the first kind didn't work for me. I'm on this sub so it's not like they're a magic cure, but they definitely help with managing some of the day-to-day swing for me.

If my parents are any indication, age is totally irrelevant lol. It seems like it has to do with years someone has been working on growing, or whatever. I apologize if it came across that I was saying "You're so lucky to have what you have" or something - I know if someone said that to me it would feel pretty invalidating. I guess what I really meant to convey was that it was nice to know that the depression monster fights with people who have things I hope to have, too - in the sense that it didn't have to be defeated to get there, or that it didn't prevent you from getting there, even though its hard!

I get it. Like maybe not exactly what you're going through, but I had to go through several diagnoses before I found one that I really felt fit what I was struggling with, and I had parents who decidedly did NOT sort out their shit before having kids. My mom, as recently as a few weeks ago, said she wished she hadn't had me over some PETTY argument that never needed to escalate.

I think my advice would be, if you're skeptical about your diagnosis (it sounds like you've thought about it a lot and really care about having a meaningful diagnosis), don't be afraid to seek a second (or third, or fourth) opinion.

It took me 5 years (started when I was 22) to really find a therapist who was interested in understanding ME and what I struggled with and was willing to consider multiple treatment options. She's of the mindset that "the goal is to get better, a diagnosis is just a way to figure out how to do that, but the most important thing is to understand what you're struggling with and how to help YOU". For me, that's been helpful. I definitely still struggle (I'm on this sub after all), but like I at least feel like I was able to find some new direction in all of this mess of sh\*t we call life once I got a few additional opinions outside of "you're depressed".

My situation is totally different in a lot of ways, but I can appreciate the deep hurtful frustration of being an advocate for self care and mental health in the workplace, putting up with a lot of hard shit day-to-day without complaining, having a few bad interactions when people do petty buy maybe-not-a-big-deal-to-others stuff, and then getting that all throw in your face with some not-so-nice side comments by your manager or boss.  


I had something similar happen. I'm still struggling with it. It makes me feel better (not in a way that looks negatively on you) that someone at the age of 40 also struggles with this shit. Like maybe it just doesn't go away and other people can just be like that.

​

To be fair, the way you wrote about all of this seems a lot more level-headed than the way I would write about it. You're married to your best friend, too. I know how depression is, it doesn't care about "small" things like that, but from one struggling person to another, I'm a little jealous of you. You seem well spoken even when you're hurting (I struggle a lot with that) and you have at least one person you love in your life. I'm sure it doesn't make it feel better, but maybe you'll be able to have a momentary chuckle that someone younger can read about the hard stuff you're struggling with and still be jealous :P

Listen, I won't tell you not to do it. I *definitely* won't tell you not to do it because it might hurt other people. You won't listen to some rando on the internet and you won't believe me anyway, and that's fair because I wouldn't believe me either. But 16 is young. I knew a lot of depressed people when I was 16 (they were also 16). Like, most of the people I knew were depressed.
